name: Uma Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the Harlow estate, have done for nineteen years. It's a big place, 400 hectares, about 250 beef cattle and a lot of potatoes. I'm the stock person, so I check the cattle first thing, sort feed, move groups between fields, and in autumn I'm on the potato harvester like everyone else. The family who own it are decent enough. Mr Harlow's son runs it now and he's keener on figures than his father was.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The potato harvest, every year. Twelve-hour days in the dust for six weeks. My partner Tom drives a delivery van for the builders' merchant, and with Elsa at fourteen and Finn at ten, somebody's always needing a lift somewhere. I don't touch any of that AI stuff. I've got enough on with the phone the estate gave me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI Plateau. That's the one where I carry on, then. Suits me, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the tea room I'd say I told you it was all talk. I'd say it to Darren and the lads and that'd be the end of it. I don't go on about things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad, but it doesn't take away young Mr Harlow. My boss, young Mr Harlow, has been looking at GPS collars for the cattle, and those collars exist whether AI is hype or not. If he buys them he doesn't need two stock people walking the fields, and I'm the one on the older contract with the higher rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the cattle and keep my head down. I'd put 150 a month aside instead of 100 and keep chipping at the mortgage. And I'd ask around quietly at Fenwick's dairy whether they ever need a stock person, just so I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, if I'm honest, though I wouldn't say it out loud. It's not the AI, it's the look young Mr Harlow gets when he's doing sums about us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom about the collars?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tom not to fret, then fret myself on the drive home. Tom's van job isn't the steadiest either, because the builders' merchant had a bad winter. We've never both been worried at once and I'd rather not start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask around. Would you actually leave Harlow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not unless I had to. Nineteen years is a long time, and I know every gate on that estate. But knowing Fenwick's would take me is the difference between sleeping and not.

say: I told you it was **all talk**.
I'd say it to **Darren and the lads** in the tea room and leave it there, because I don't go on.
think: I'd be glad, but young Mr Harlow is still looking at **GPS collars** for the cattle.
With those he doesn't need **two stock people**, and I'm on the older contract with the higher rate.
do: Carries on with the cattle and **keeps her head down**.
Raises savings from 100 to **150 a month** while chipping at the mortgage.
Asks quietly at **Fenwick's dairy** whether they ever need a stock person.
feel: **Anxious** under a **calm face**, not because of AI but because of her boss's sums about the staff.
S0.quote: My boss, young Mr Harlow, has been looking at GPS collars for the cattle, and those collars exist whether AI is hype or not.
fieldNote: Uma separates AI hype from **the collars** her boss is already pricing, which could cut the stock team to one.
Her **higher pay** after nineteen years makes her feel more exposed, not less.
Tom's employer had **a bad winter** too, so both household incomes feel shaky.

steps.text: Keep doing the cattle rounds at Harlow and keep her head down
Raise savings from 100 to 150 a month
Ask quietly at Fenwick's dairy about stock work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office stuff goes first. The estate office is where young Mr Harlow does his sums, so that's where it starts for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, there's always change and you get on with it. If the lads asked, I'd say a computer can't pull a calf. That's all I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's the collars plus the office software. A computer that plans the grazing tells my boss in black and white that one stock person is enough. It's me or Kieran, and Kieran is twenty-six and costs less. Tom's driving is safe enough, but the builders' merchant would have fewer people on the counter and less overtime going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd raise savings to 200 a month straight away and put the holiday off. I'd ask young Mr Harlow plainly, in the first month, what he's planning, which I've never done in nineteen years. And I'd go and see Fenwick's properly, not just ask around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be lying awake doing his sums for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Elsa and Finn notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elsa would notice the holiday, because she's fourteen and notices everything. Finn would just notice I'm short-tempered at tea. I'd tell Elsa the truth if she asked, she's old enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You never use AI. Would you learn the grazing software to stay on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it kept my job, I'd sit with it, yes, but I'd hate it. I'd rather young Mr Harlow saw me as the one who knows Biscuit's moods than the one who can work his tablet. That's probably the wrong answer.

say: Change always comes and you **get on with it**.
A computer **can't pull a calf**, and that's all I'd say about it.
think: Grazing software plus the collars tells my boss that **one stock person** is enough.
It's me or **Kieran**, who's younger and cheaper.
Tom's driving is safe, but **his overtime** would thin out.
do: Raises savings to **200 a month** at once and puts off the family holiday.
Asks young Mr Harlow **directly** in the first month what he's planning.
feel: **Anxious**, lying awake doing her boss's sums for him.
S1.quote: A computer that plans the grazing tells my boss in black and white that one stock person is enough.
fieldNote: Uma linked the card straight to her job: with **grazing software**, the case for two stock people falls apart.
She expects the **younger, cheaper colleague** to be kept.
For someone who never asks questions, planning to **confront her boss** was a big step.

steps.text: Raise savings to 200 a month straight away
Put off this year's family holiday
Visit Fenwick's dairy properly about a stock person's job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office goes first and the field after. That's three years, then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the tea room I'd say the cattle still need a person for now, and the robots are three years off, so no point panicking. I'd say it to Darren and the lads on the harvester. I wouldn't say anything else, I don't go on about things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the first thing that goes in 2028 is the office, and the office is where young Mr Harlow does his sums. A computer that plans the grazing better than me tells him exactly how few people he needs, and he'd have the numbers ready for when the robots come in 2031. Tom's van is the same, someone has to carry the timber for now, and then nobody does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard straight away, no holiday, and Elsa's school trip to the coast would have to go. We'd put about 250 a month on the mortgage so it's smaller by 2031. I'd ask young Mr Harlow straight out whether there's a job for me after the robots, which I've never done in nineteen years. I'd let Tom look for something steadier first, because his van goes at the same time as my cattle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, if I'm honest. I'd lie awake doing sums, and the three years would feel like a countdown, not a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Elsa about the school trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the truth, that money's tight and it might get tighter. My daughter would be upset for a day about the school trip, and then she'd tell me it didn't matter, which would be worse. She's fourteen, she'd understand more than I'd want her to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Mr Harlow straight out. What do you think he'd say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He’d say something like ‘let’s see how it goes, Uma’, which means no. He’s not a bad man. Young Mr Harlow would already have the computer’s figures on how few stock people the estate needs in a folder on his desk.

say: The cattle still need **a person for now**, and the robots are three years off.
There's **no point panicking**, and that's all I'd say in the tea room.
think: The **estate office** goes first in 2028, and a computer that plans grazing tells my boss how few people he needs.
**Tom's delivery van** is on the same 2031 clock.
do: **Cuts spending** at once, dropping the holiday and Elsa's school trip.
Puts about **250 a month** on the mortgage before 2031.
Asks young Mr Harlow **directly** about a job after the robots, and lets Tom look for steadier work first.
feel: **Sick with worry**, lying awake doing sums.
The three years would feel like **a countdown**, not a cushion.
S2.quote: Young Mr Harlow would already have the computer’s figures on how few stock people the estate needs in a folder on his desk.
fieldNote: Uma read the three-year gap as **a countdown** rather than a breathing space.
She expects the estate's AI planning to be used to **decide who stays** when the robots come.
She'd ask the owner about her future for **the first time** in nineteen years, already expecting no.

steps.text: Cancel the family holiday and Elsa's school trip to the coast
Put about 250 a month on the mortgage before the robots come in 2031
Let Tom look for steadier work than the van first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the office, eight for the field. I'd be 51.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, there's always change and you get on with it. If people at the estate asked, I'd tell them there's eight years before a robot can move a herd. That's a long time in farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still the same ending, just with more time to watch it coming. I'd be 51 when the robots arrive, Elsa would be grown and Finn nearly. I think I'd spend five years watching the estate office change and three more waiting for the field to follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd save as hard as we can, about 200 a month, and I'd sell the second car when it needs its next big repair. I'd wait and see what the estate actually buys in 2031 before doing anything else. I'd make sure Elsa takes her exams seriously, because I want her to have more choices than I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but slowly. It's like a bad tooth you know you'll have to deal with one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning the new machines this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the estate paid for it and gave me the time, maybe. I'm not going to the college in the evenings at fifty to sit with teenagers. I know that's stubborn, Tom tells me so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Elsa to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something where people need people. Nursing, maybe, or the vet's. I'd like my daughter to have a job where somebody's glad to see her come through the door.

say: There's always change and you **get on with it**.
There's **eight years** before a robot can move a herd, and that's a long time in farming.
think: It's **the same ending** with more time to watch it coming, and I'd be 51 when the robots arrive.
I'd spend five years watching **the estate office** change and three more waiting for the field.
do: Saves about **200 a month** and plans to sell the second car at its next big repair.
**Waits to see** what the estate buys in 2031 before acting.
Makes sure **Elsa takes her exams** seriously.
feel: **Anxious, but slowly**, like a bad tooth she knows she'll have to deal with one day.
S3.quote: I'd like my daughter to have a job where somebody's glad to see her come through the door.
fieldNote: Uma still **won't retrain** unless the estate pays and gives her the time, and she owns that stubbornness.
The extra years mostly let her **save** and get her children through school.
Her hopes for her daughter are about **being needed by people** rather than money.

steps.text: Save about 200 a month and sell the second car at its next repair
Wait to see what machines the Harlow estate buys in 2031
Make sure Elsa takes her exams seriously

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039 for the robots. Finn would be twenty-three. That's different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and anything can happen. People said the same about the milking machines once. In the tea room I'd probably just shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be 56 by the time a robot could do my job, and the children would be grown. That's not retirement, but it's not starting out either. The office would change from 2036 and I wouldn't miss the paperwork one bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the cattle and keep putting 150 a month by, and pay the mortgage down when I can. I'd steer Elsa and Finn towards something solid. I wouldn't learn anything new unless the estate asked me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, now and then. Mostly I'd be thinking about the kids, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by something solid for the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I used to say a trade, plumbing or electrics. But if robots can do hands-on work by 2039, even that's not certain. If even a trade isn't safe, I don't really know what to tell my kids, and that's the honest answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Biscuit, your cow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Biscuit would be long gone by then, she's twelve already. That's a strange thought, that my favourite cow won't live to see it.

say: Ten years is **a long time** and anything can happen.
People said the same about **the milking machines** once.
think: I'd be **56** by the time a robot could do my job, with the children grown.
The **office paperwork** changing from 2036 is something I wouldn't miss.
do: Carries on with the cattle and keeps putting **150 a month** by.
Pays **the mortgage** down when she can.
Steers Elsa and Finn towards **solid work** and learns nothing new unless the estate asks.
feel: **Uneasy now and then**, mostly about the children rather than herself.
S4.quote: If even a trade isn't safe, I don't really know what to tell my kids, and that's the honest answer.
fieldNote: With thirteen years before robots, Uma's worry moves almost entirely onto **her children**.
Her old advice to **learn a trade** no longer works, and she has nothing to replace it.
She'd keep working as she is **without retraining**.

steps.text: Keep looking after the Harlow estate's beef cattle as she does now
Keep putting 150 a month by and pay the mortgage down
Steer Elsa and Finn towards work that will still need people

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Tom's van and my cattle would both go to the robots by 2031, and three years isn't long enough for someone like me to find somewhere to go. What would help is money from the government to tide families over, quickly, and someone telling me plainly what jobs there'd be for someone like me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what the cattle would think. I know that sounds daft. But I've got a cow called Biscuit who follows me round the field, and no collar's going to get that.

headlineQuote: I've got a cow called Biscuit who follows me round the field, and no collar's going to get that.
portrait: Uma Jensen, 43, has been **stock person** on the large Harlow estate for nineteen years, with beef cattle and potatoes.
She **never uses AI** and keeps her head down, treating change as plain business.
Even if AI stalls she's **anxious**, because her boss is pricing GPS collars that would leave room for one stock person.
Steady change adds **grazing software**, so she'd save harder, ask him outright and look at a nearby dairy.
Fast AGI **alarms** her for her job and Tom's; with more time her worry moves to her children.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and her partner would both lose their hands-on jobs to robots by 2031.
There'd be **too little time** to find other work.
whatWouldHelp: **Quick government money** to tide families over.
Someone telling her **plainly** what work would exist for someone like her.
